newsitem.title: USA: Lead concs market faces huge oversupply - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Lead concs market faces huge oversupply - analyst.

text.p: The lead concentrates market faces a big oversupply and miners may find it difficult to sell their output, an analyst said.
"There is actually quite an alarming picture developing in lead concentrates," analyst Huw Roberts of Brook Hunt told the American Zinc Association conference.
Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd will bring on stream its Cannington mine shortly, adding 165,000 tonnes of contained lead in concentrates to an already oversupplied market.
Lead and zinc are often mined from the same deposit. About half the world's lead demand is met from recycled lead.

"Bear in mind this is a market for concentrates which is little over two million tonnes a year of lead content," Roberts said. "I can actually forsee a situation in 1998 and 1999 where there will be a substantial increase in lead concentrates."

Some miners will face problems selling their concentrates in such an oversupplied market "at any treatment charge whatsoever", Roberts said. "The capacity is certainly not in the Western system to absorb the increase in lead concentrates which is going to be coming through."

"This does beg the question very seriously, what happens to those zinc mines which are very dependent on lead concentrates. We need more zinc concentrates, we don't need more lead concentrates," Roberts added. "Typically you don't get one without the other."

Metaleurop and Cominco settled their zinc concentrate benchmark price for 1997 earlier on Wednesday, and Metaleurop's board member Christian Bue said settlements for lead concentrates did not represent any major difficulty.
"Lead will be settled easily with an improvement in favor of the smelters compared to last year," Bue told Reuters.
In 1996 lead treatment charges were settled at $170-$175 per tonne, basis LME cash lead price of $600 per tonne.
